title: Coral and the Glasshouse
premise: Lior Oyelaran, a bridge inspector who measures everything in tolerances and expansion joints, has spent eleven years cataloguing the silences in their marriage to Ada. When a box of undelivered letters—written by Lior during the worst year, never sent—surfaces behind a wardrobe, the couple is forced into an audit of every grievance they've stored instead of spoken. As the house sale closes in six weeks, they read the letters aloud one by one, discovering that Ada knew about the affair the letters confess, and chose silence as her own form of loyalty. The novel ends not with reconciliation or divorce but with something rarer: a proper goodbye to the marriage they actually had, spoken out loud on the empty porch before the new owners arrive.
about_author: Zephyrine Underhill is a former structural engineer who left bridge inspection after fifteen years to write fiction about the loads people carry. She lives in a coastal town where she still cannot pass a span without checking its bearings.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A routine inspection of the Harrow Street overpass opens the novel: Lior measures cracks, records deflections, and privately maps the same method onto their marriage. At home, Ada has begun packing for the house sale without discussing it. The emotional beat is quiet dread—the sense of a structure holding, barely, under weight no one has declared.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Moving a wardrobe to stage the house for sale, Ada finds a shoebox taped behind the backing panel: forty-one letters, addressed to her, in Lior's handwriting, all unopened, spanning one terrible year. She reads three before Lior comes home. The beat is vertigo—grief arriving years late, with interest.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Confronted, Lior admits writing the letters during the year of the affair with Tomas and the year of near-silence after; sending them felt like detonation. Ada reveals she found them once before, years ago, and put them back unread. The beat is mutual exposure: both kept archives, both lied by omission.

chapters.title: Expansion Joint
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Flashback chapter to year four: how Ada learned of the affair from a neighbor's careless remark and said nothing, testing whether Lior would confess. Lior never did. Ada explains this now, flatly, over unpacked boxes. The beat is cold clarity—the moment loyalty curdles into surveillance.

chapters.title: Forty-One
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. They agree to a protocol: one letter read aloud per evening until the sale closes, then a final conversation. Lior dreads letter nineteen above all. The beat is grim ceremony—two engineers designing a procedure for collapse.

chapters.title: Letters One Through Six
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The early letters are almost tender—apologies circling without landing, descriptions of bridges as metaphors for distance. Ada listens with a stenographer's face. Between readings, they sort belongings, arguing over a lamp neither wants. The beat is false calm; the ritual feels survivable, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

chapters.title: Tomas
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Letter nine names Tomas directly. Lior describes the affair not as passion but as relief—being seen without translation. Ada asks only logistical questions: when, where, how long. Her restraint terrifies Lior more than rage would. The beat is shame without absolution.

chapters.title: What the Neighbor Said
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada finally tells her side of year four: the remark at the school fundraiser, the drive home beside a silent spouse, the months of watching for a confession that never came. She describes composing her own unsent letter and burning it. The beat is symmetrical ruin—both were writing the same document in different hands.

chapters.title: Letter Fourteen
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Letter fourteen confesses the night Lior stood outside their own house, unable to come in, and drove to Tomas's instead. Reading it aloud, Lior watches Ada realize the timeline matches the night her father died. The beat is catastrophic timing—grief discovering it was abandoned at its worst hour.

chapters.title: The Sale
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The buyer's solicitor accelerates the closing date; the deadline compresses. Ada considers halting the readings, calling the whole thing off, selling and scattering. Instead she insists they continue, faster. The beat is perverse resolve—if the marriage must be demolished, she wants to watch it fall honestly.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, following Lior. Lior's sister Nkechi arrives to help pack and senses the fracture, pushing reconciliation clichés that both resent. Lior nearly tells her everything, then doesn't. The beat is the loneliness of private justice—outsiders offering law where the couple needs something else entirely.

chapters.title: Letters Twenty Through Twenty-Five
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Mid-box, the letters turn angry: Lior blaming Ada's silence for the affair's duration. Ada answers each aloud with corrections of fact, a line-by-line rebuttal she has carried for a decade. The beat is escalation—the ritual becoming a trial neither presides over.

chapters.title: Bearing Failure
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada reveals her own secret held through the same year: a pregnancy ended alone while Lior was away, never mentioned since. The readings halt. Lior understands, for the first time, the weight Ada carried in parallel. The beat is stunned recalibration—the ledger was never one-sided.

chapters.title: Letter Thirty-One
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Letter thirty-one is the last before the affair ended: a proposal to leave the marriage, written and never sent because Tomas refused to be anyone's rescue. Lior reads it and hears, in their own old voice, someone they no longer recognize. The beat is estrangement from the self—the past as foreign country.

chapters.title: Nineteen
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada has secretly read letter nineteen alone. It contains the sentence Lior feared most: 'I think I stopped loving you and didn't notice.' Ada chooses whether to demand it be read. She does. The beat is deliberate wounding as honesty—justice administered by hand.

chapters.title: The Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. With most rooms bare, the couple sleeps on a mattress in the kitchen and reads letters by work light. The stripped house becomes a confessional. They begin answering the letters' questions ten years late, conversation outrunning the documents. The beat is strange intimacy—closeness possible only inside demolition.

chapters.title: Tomas Returns
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Tomas, now ill, sends a message asking to see Lior. Lior visits and finds not a rival but a tired man who remembers the year differently—as the loneliest of his life. Lior leaves without resolution. The beat is disillusionment; the escape hatch was never a door.

chapters.title: Letter Forty-One
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The final letter, written after the affair ended, asks nothing and apologizes for everything—a surrender Ada never received and therefore never answered. Reading it, she weeps for the first time in the book. The beat is grief finally given its appointment, a decade overdue.

chapters.title: Closing Day Eve
chapters.summary: Third-person limited. All boxes gone, keys on the counter, the couple sits on the porch floor with wine in jam jars. They attempt the final conversation and fail twice—retreating into logistics, into blame—before Lior says the true thing: not 'I'm sorry' but 'I should have let you know me.' The beat is the threshold crossed.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Properly
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The goodbye itself: they speak the marriage's eulogy together, sentence by sentence, naming what it was—refuge, fortress, prison—and releasing each other from the debts of silence. No decision about divorce is made; the ending is the honesty, not the paperwork. The beat is ceremonial release.

chapters.title: Handover
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Morning: the buyers arrive, cheerful, measuring curtains. Ada and Lior walk the house one last time, leaving the wardrobe behind deliberately, its backing panel open—an archive offered to whoever comes next. On the sidewalk they shake hands like colleagues. The beat is bittersweet civility, love's afterimage.

chapters.title: Deflection
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, epilogue. Months later, inspecting a new span, Lior finds a hairline crack and writes the report truthfully, flagging it for repair rather than tolerance. That evening, Lior mails a letter—this time stamped and addressed—to Ada, containing no apology, only news. The beat is earned hope: speech as ongoing practice, justice as maintenance.
